questions.q: What guarantees does UDP NOT provide that TCP does?
options: Guaranteed delivery, guaranteed ordering, and automatic retransmission of lost packets
The ability to use port numbers
A valid IP address format
The ability to send any data at all
questions.explain: UDP sends self-contained datagrams with no handshake and no guarantee they arrive, arrive in order, or get retransmitted if lost -- all guarantees TCP provides.

questions.q: Why do real exchange market-data feeds use UDP multicast rather than TCP, despite UDP's lack of reliability guarantees?
options: Multicast lets the sender transmit one packet that the network replicates to every subscriber, which has a fundamentally cheaper cost structure than TCP's one connection and one message copy per subscriber at exchange scale
UDP is simply newer technology than TCP and therefore always preferred
UDP guarantees faster delivery than TCP in every single case
TCP cannot be used to send numeric price data
questions.explain: At the scale of thousands of subscribers, one-to-many multicast delivery (send once, network replicates) is a different cost structure than TCP's one-to-one connections -- this is the real reason, not raw speed.

questions.q: Since UDP guarantees nothing about delivery, who is responsible for detecting a gap (a lost packet) in a UDP market-data feed?
options: UDP automatically detects and retransmits lost packets, identically to TCP
The network switch silently repairs any lost packets before they are counted as lost
The receiving application itself, typically by tracking sequence numbers embedded in the application-level message format
Gaps in UDP are impossible by design
questions.explain: UDP provides no gap detection on its own -- the receiving application has to track sequence numbers itself and decide whether to tolerate the loss or request a retransmission through a separate channel.

questions.q: What problem does marking a socket non-blocking solve, and what new problem does it introduce?
options: It eliminates the need to check return values from send() or recv()
It makes TCP behave exactly like UDP
It stops recv() from blocking the calling thread when no data is ready, but introduces the question of how one thread efficiently knows which of many sockets actually has data ready
It guarantees the socket will always have data ready to read
questions.explain: Non-blocking I/O removes the thread-per-connection blocking problem, but a thread now needs an efficient way to discover which of many sockets is actually ready -- which is exactly what select()/poll()/epoll() solve.

questions.q: Why is epoll() generally preferred over select() or poll() for a server handling thousands of concurrent connections?
options: epoll() automatically multiplies the number of connections a server can accept
epoll() is available on more operating systems than select() or poll()
epoll() lets the kernel maintain the interest list persistently and only returns sockets that actually became ready, avoiding the full-list rescan that select() and poll() repeat on every call
select() and poll() cannot monitor more than one socket at a time
questions.explain: select() and poll() rescan the entire monitored list on every call (and select() also caps how many descriptors it can track); epoll()'s persistent interest list and ready-only results are what make it scale to thousands of connections.
